preview: Hrim Gandhi's FTE interview experience at Goldman Sachs covers the online test, technical rounds focusing on DSA and LLD, and the HR + technical round leading to an offer.
content:
FTE Interview Experience
Goldman Sachs
Hrim Gandhi, B.Tech CS 2018-22
Part 1: Online Test (Aptitude):
The online test took place on 1st August, 2021. More than 200 students from different branches gave the test. It was conducted on HackerRank and was divided into different sections. Each section had a separate timer, and we weren’t allowed to attempt questions from the previous sections once the timer ran out.
It consisted of five sections:
1. 2 Coding Questions (30 mins)
2. 8 MCQs (20 mins). They were based on:
● PnC and Probability
● Integration and Area under the Curve
● Trigonometry and basic math formulae taught in 11th and 12th
Tip: Don’t take MCQs lightly. Sometimes they can be a deciding factor for getting shortlisted. There was negative marking for incorrect answers to MCQs, so read the instructions well.
3. Advanced Coding Question (45 mins)
4. 2 Essay type situation based questions (15 mins)
● Describe a time when your passion and energy led to your team's victory.
● You are in a team of two members, and your co-team member cannot work on the project that needs to be completed before a certain deadline. What will you do in this situation?
Tip: These questions are very common in Goldman Sachs' online assessment, so you can prepare them beforehand.
5. 7 MCQs (20 mins), based on CS related subjects
● Computer Networks
● OS
● Programming language, OOPS

Coding Questions
The coding questions were of medium to hard difficulty level. The difficulty of the questions may vary drastically each year.
a. Section 1
1. Given an array of length N, each element in the array represents the strength of a badminton player. Matches are scheduled such that consecutive players compete with each other. The player with more strength wins, and if the strengths are equal, the second player wins and proceeds to the next round. Then the winners compete with each other till there is only one player left. We had to print the maximum level each player could reach.
It was mentioned that length is of the form 2*N (ideally should have been 2^N)
Input: N = 4, Array = [1, 4, 2, 3]
Output: [0, 2, 0, 1]
2. Given an array of strings, each string has some value. If you can form a sentence which can have upto 30 characters, maximise the value by choosing strings from the array. Each string in the sentence will be separated by a space and each space will be counted as one character.
Input: N = 4, Array = [“priorityqueue”, “linkedlist”, “binarytree”, “adjacencymatrix”], Values = [5, 6, 9, 10]
Output: 19
Explanation: When the last two strings from the array are selected, the sentence formed will be of length 10+1+15 = 26.
Tip: Although I didn't realise it at the moment, it was a standard 01 knapsack question. Carefully look at the constraints in such tests. Sometimes a brute-force or a recursive solution will also work for many test cases.

b. Section 3 (Advanced)
Given a graph, we can apply the operation an arbitrary number of times (possibly 0) to transform the given graph into a Complete Graph . An operation is defined as follows.
1. Pick any vertex from the graph.
2. Remove all pre existing edges from the vertex to other vertices.
3. Add edges to all other vertices except the ones we removed in the previous step.
We have to figure out whether it's possible to obtain a complete graph from the given graph by applying the operation an arbitrary number of times.
Input Graph:
Output: Complete Graph Possible
Explanation: We have 3 nodes (1, 2 and 3) and have only 1 edge between nodes 1 and 2. We choose node 1, so the existing edge is removed, and the remaining edges are added. Then we finally select node 2, and the 2 remaining edges are added and we have a complete graph.
Tip: Go through the questions that you weren’t able to solve or think of an optimal approach for a question that you had solved in the online test. Sometimes you can expect a discussion or follow up questions from the online test during your interviews.

Part 2: Technical Interviews
There were 2 technical interviews which consisted of DSA and OOPs design questions. The interviews were held on a zoom video call, and we were asked to code on HackerRank Codepair during the interviews. 11 people had been shortlisted for this round.
Round 1: Technical
My interview started with the basic tell-me-about-yourself question.
Tip: This is always going to be the first question in all the interviews you give, so prepare a crisp introduction that you can use everywhere. The things you say can guide your interview from here on. For example, if you say you are more into development, you can expect follow up questions on your projects. Also, you can mention your internships, hackathons and positions of responsibility.
I was asked some questions like: "Why would you want to work for Goldman Sachs?", "How do you think Goldman Sachs makes money?" and "What would you choose － Goldman Sachs or Google?". Make sure you do your research about the company.
He then moved on to asking me a DSA question:
Given an array of N elements and a positive integer K where each element is in the range [1, K). Print the frequency of each number lying in the range [1, K).
I started with the brute force approach and then optimised it further. I wasn't asked to write the code for this question.
Tip: Think out loud. Explain your logic before you move on to the code. Even if you are stuck on a question, build up your approach and explain as you think. Listen carefully to the interviewer, generally they give you hints when you are stuck somewhere. Having said that, don’t ask for help yourself, explain your approach and work on that.
After this, he asked me if I had any questions for him. I asked him questions about the work culture at Goldman Sachs and the projects that they work on.
Out of 11 students, 6 were shortlisted for the next round.

Round 2: Technical
The round, as always, began with the tell-me-about-yourself question. He explained to me that this was a design round and I will be given 20 minutes to design a chess game.
This was more of a discussion round, so I went step by step. First, I identified the requirements and the classes. Then I moved to entities, their attributes and then the methods. Low Level Design (OOPs) was expected and I wasn't asked much about System Design.
He asked me if I had any questions and this concluded my second round.

Part 3: HR + Technical Round
This round was conducted only for 3 candidates out of the 6.
My interview began with an introduce-yourself question. This was followed by an HR round and the questions mainly revolved around where I would like to work and why－"Google or Goldman Sachs". Questions got trickier but I answered them with flair (and with confidence xD).
In the technical section, I was asked a question based on BFS and a puzzle.
1. Given a source and a destination coordinate on a chessboard, find the minimum number of moves a knight will have to make to reach from the source to the destination.
2. A person has 4000 bananas and a camel. What is the maximum number of bananas that a person can transfer to a destination which is 1000 kms away, using only the camel as a mode of transportation. The camel cannot carry more than 1000 bananas at a time and eats a banana every km it travels.
In the end, she asked me if I had any questions for her. I asked her, “What would be the one thing that you would like to improve about Goldman Sachs?”
Tip: Always ask questions. It shows your interest in the company as well as displays your communication skills and confidence.

Results
Out of 3, 2 candidates were offered FTE Roles and I was one of them :)
Tip: The key point is to always be prepared for everything and stay calm in between the rounds. You may be called at any moment for your next round, and you may even have to wait for several hours to get the results. So be patient (or not xD) and enjoy the process.

Preparation
For DSA preparation:
● interviewbit.com
● Most common interview questions on leetcode.com (categories: easy, medium, hard)
● geeksforgeeks.com
For OOPs Design:
● https://crack-oop-system-design.herokuapp.com/
Other Interview Prep Resources:
● https://github.com/yash0530/InterviewPrepResources
Whenever you are preparing for an interview, reading company specific archives from GeeksForGeeks and about interview experiences helps a lot. You will get a basic idea of the kind and domain of the questions asked.
Different questions about your projects can be asked.
Questions on core subjects apart from DSA like OS, DBMS, CN, etc can be asked as well. I was lucky in that case because for the majority of rounds I was asked DSA based questions. This totally depends on your interviewer and your luck.
Lastly, it’s okay to be nervous. It’s okay to not stay calm. But don’t let it affect your interview. Be confident about yourself and everything shall go well.
All the Best!
